literal: Socrates: Why at-this-hour have-you-arrived, O Crito? Or is-it not still early?
prose: Socrates: Why have you come at this hour, Crito? Or is it still early?

literal: Crito. Very much indeed then.
prose: Crito: Certainly, indeed.

literal: Socrates: What-time especially?
prose: Socrates: What time is it, roughly?

literal: Crito: [It is] deep dawn.
prose: Crito: It is early dawn.

literal: Socrates: I marvel how the guard of the prison was willing to give heed to you.
prose: Socrates: I'm amazed that the prison guard was willing to listen to you.

literal: Crito. Familiar already to-me he-is, O Socrates, on-account-of the often here to-visit, and something too has-been-benefited by me.
prose: Crito: He's already on familiar terms with me, Socrates, because of his coming here often, and he's been done some good turn by me too.

literal: Socrates. Just-now δὲ have-you-come, or long-ago [have you come]?
prose: Socrates: Have you just now arrived, or have you been here a long time?

literal: Crito. Fairly early, long ago.
prose: Crito: Fairly early, quite a while ago.

literal: Socrates. Then, how did you not wake me at once, but sit beside [me] in silence?
prose: Socrates: Then why didn't you wake me at once, instead of sitting there beside me in silence?

literal: Crito. Not, by Zeus, O Socrates, not indeed would I myself have wanted to be in so-great both sleeplessness and grief, but also of-you long-since I-marvel, perceiving how pleasantly you-sleep; and on-purpose you not I-woke, in-order-that as most-pleasantly you-might-pass-the-time. And often indeed both before too, in the whole life, I-counted-happy you for-the character, but especially in the now standing-by misfortune, how easily it and gently you-bear.
prose: Crito: No, by Zeus, Socrates, I myself would not want to be in so much sleeplessness and grief; but indeed I have long been marveling at you, noticing how pleasantly you sleep. And I woke you on purpose, so that you might spend the time as pleasantly as possible. And often before too, in your whole life, I have counted you fortunate for your character, but especially now in the misfortune that has come upon you, seeing how easily and gently you bear it.

literal: Socrates: For indeed it would be, O Crito, unseemly [for one] to be vexed, being so old, if it is necessary already to be dying.
prose: Socrates: For indeed, Crito, it would be unseemly for one my age to be vexed if I must now die.

literal: Crito: And also others, O Socrates, [being] so old, in such misfortunes are caught, but nothing them does age release from not being angry at the present fortune.
prose: Crito: And others too, Socrates, just as old, are caught in such misfortunes, but their age does nothing at all to keep them from being upset at their present fortune.

literal: Socrates: These things are [so]. But why then so early have-you-arrived?
prose: Socrates: That is so. But why have you come so early?

literal: Crito: a message, O Socrates, bearing [it], hard—not for you, as to me it appears, but for me and for your friends, for all, both hard and heavy—which I, as to me it seems, among the heaviest [things] would bear.
prose: Crito: [I bring] a hard message, Socrates, not hard for you, as it seems to me, but hard and heavy for me and for all your friends—one which I, as it seems to me, would bear among the heaviest.

literal: Socrates. [What is] this, what [thing do you mean]? Or the ship has-arrived from Delos, upon-the-arrival of-which it-is-necessary [for] me to-have-died?
prose: Socrates: What ever do you mean by this? Or has the ship arrived from Delos, upon whose arrival I am to die?

literal: Crito: Surely-not indeed has-it-arrived, but it-seems on-the-one-hand to-me it-will-come today from-the-things-which they-report, some having-arrived from Sunium and having-left it there.
prose: Crito: It certainly hasn't arrived yet, but it seems to me it will come today, judging from what some people report who have arrived from Sunium and left it there.

literal: Socrates: But, O Crito, with good fortune, if in this way [it is] pleasing to the gods, in this way let it be. Not however I-think it to-be-going-to-arrive today.
prose: Socrates: Well then, Crito, with good fortune, if this is pleasing to the gods in this way, so let it be. But I don't think it will arrive today.

literal: Crito: Socrates: From where do you infer this?
prose: Crito: Socrates: From what do you infer this?

literal: Socrates: For, presumably, on-the next-day it-is-necessary [for] me to-die, or on-which [day] should-come the ship.
prose: Socrates: For presumably I must die on the next day, or on whichever day the ship arrives.

literal: Crito: They say indeed, you know, [that] those in authority over these things [can].
prose: Crito: They say, at any rate, that those who have authority over these matters can do so.

literal: Socrates: Not, then, on-the coming day, I-think, will it come, but on-the other [day]. I-conjecture, moreover, from a certain dream which I-have-seen a-little before, of-this the night; and you-risk, at some not [good] moment, to-wake me.
prose: Socrates: Not, I think, on the coming day, but on the next one. And I judge this from a certain dream I saw a little earlier tonight; and you may well be waking me at rather an unfortunate moment.

literal: Crito: [It] was, then, indeed, what the dream?
prose: Crito: Well then, what was the dream?

literal: Socrates. It seemed [to me] a certain woman, having approached, beautiful and fair-formed, wearing white garments, to call me and to say: O Socrates, on the third day might you come to fertile Phthia.
prose: Socrates: A woman seemed to come up to me, beautiful and fair, wearing white garments, and to call me and say, "O Socrates, on the third day you might reach fertile Phthia."

literal: Crito: [It is] strange, the dream, O Socrates.
prose: Crito: That's a strange dream, Socrates.

literal: Socrates: Clear indeed then, as it seems to me at least, O Crito, [it is].
prose: Socrates: Well, it is clear, at least as it seems to me, Crito.

literal: Crito. Too [true] indeed, as it seems. But, O strange Socrates, still even now obey me and be saved; as to me, if you should die, [it is] not one misfortune, but apart from having been deprived of such a friend, of the sort of which I myself shall never find anyone, still moreover to many I shall seem—to those who do not clearly know both me and you—[namely] that, being able to save you, if I had been willing to spend money, [I] neglected [you].
prose: Crito: Too much so indeed, it seems. But, my strange Socrates, even now listen to me and save yourself; since for me, if you should die, it would not be a single misfortune, but besides being deprived of such a friend as I shall never find another like, I shall also seem to many—those who do not know you and me well—to have neglected you, since I could have saved you if I had been willing to spend money.

literal: And-yet what could be more-shameful than this, opinion, than to-seem money about more to-make than friends? For not will-be-persuaded the many, that you yourself were-not-willing to-depart from-here, we being-eager.
prose: And yet what opinion could be more shameful than this—to seem to value money more than friends? For most people won't believe that you yourself were unwilling to leave this place, even though we were eager for it.

literal: Socrates: But why to us, O blessed Crito, does [there] so much care of the opinion of the many [belong]?
prose: Socrates: But, my dear blessed Crito, why should we care so much about the opinion of the majority?

literal: Crito. But you see, indeed, Socrates, that [it is] necessary also to care for the opinion of the many. And [these] present [things] themselves [are] clear now, because the many are of such a sort as to work out not the smallest of evils but the greatest, pretty nearly, if someone among them has been slandered.
prose: Crito: But you see, Socrates, that it's also necessary to care about the opinion of the majority. The very circumstances now before us make it clear that the majority are capable of inflicting not the smallest evils, but pretty much the greatest, if someone has been slandered among them.

literal: Socrates: For would that, O Crito, the many were able to do the greatest evils, in order that they might also be able [to do] the greatest goods, [it would] indeed [have] well.
prose: Socrates: For if only ordinary people were capable of doing the greatest harm, Crito, so that they might also be capable of doing the greatest good, things would be splendid.

literal: Crito. These things indeed thus let it hold; but tell me this, O Socrates, are you not perhaps taking-thought for me and for the other friends, lest, if you should go out from here, the informers cause troubles for us, [saying] that [they] stole you out from here, and [we] be compelled either also to lose all the property or much money, or also to suffer some other thing besides these things?
prose: Crito. Well then, let's leave things as they are. But tell me this, Socrates: are you not perhaps worried about me and about your other friends, in case, if you should escape from here, the informers give us trouble by claiming that we smuggled you out of here, and we're forced either to lose all our property, or a great deal of money, or even to suffer something else besides these things?

literal: Crito. For if you fear some such [thing], let it go [bid it farewell]; for we, I suppose, are just [men], having saved you, to run this risk, and if it be necessary, still [risks] greater than this.
prose: Crito: For if you're afraid of some such thing, let it go. For we, I suppose, are justified in saving you and running this risk, and if need be, even greater risks than this.

literal: Socrates: And these things I-am-considering, O Crito, and other many [things].
prose: Socrates: These are the things I'm worried about, Crito, and many others besides.

literal: Crito: And don't you worry, then, about this — for not indeed much is the money which certain men, having taken [it], are willing both to save you and to lead [you] out from here. Then don't you see these informers, how cheap [they are], and nothing would be needed against them of much money? To you indeed there is available, as I think, the my money, sufficient. Then also, if indeed caring for anything of me, you do not think [it] necessary to spend the[se] things [of] mine, these foreigners here [are] ready to spend [theirs].
prose: Crito: So don't worry about that — the money that some men are willing to take in order to save you and get you out of here isn't even all that much. Then besides, don't you see how cheap these informers are, and how little money we'd need to deal with them? You have my money available, I think, which is enough. Then too, even if out of concern for me you don't think you ought to spend my money, these foreigners here are ready to spend theirs.

literal: So that, which very thing I say, both not fearing these things may you grow weary to save yourself, and not — what you were saying in the court — let it become distressing to you, that you would not have [anything], having gone out, that you might use yourself [for]; for in many places indeed, if also to another place, wherever you should arrive, they will welcome you.
prose: So — just what I'm saying — don't, out of fear of this, grow weary of saving yourself; and don't let it trouble you, as you said in court, that once you've gotten out you wouldn't know what to do with yourself; for in many places, wherever else you go, people will welcome you warmly.

literal: And if you wish to go into Thessaly, there are for me there guest-friends who will make [you] of much [account] and will provide safety for you, so that you no one of those throughout Thessaly [will] trouble. Still further, O Socrates, not indeed just to me do you seem to attempt a deed, [namely] to betray yourself, it being possible [for you] to be saved, and such things you hasten about yourself to become as indeed even your enemies would hasten and did hasten you to destroy, wishing [it].
prose: And if you wish to go to Thessaly, I have guest-friends there who will value you highly and will provide you with safety, so that no one in Thessaly will trouble you. And besides, Socrates, I don't think what you're attempting to do is even just—betraying yourself when it's possible for you to be saved—and you are hastening to bring such things upon yourself as even your enemies would hasten, and did hasten, to do, wishing to destroy you.

literal: And in addition to these things, also you seem to me to be betraying your own sons, whom, it being possible for you both to raise and to educate [them], you will be gone, having abandoned [them]; and, as for your part, whatever they happen [to get], this they will do/fare. And they will meet, as is the likely [thing], with such things as are accustomed to happen in orphanhoods concerning the orphans. For either it is not necessary to make children, or [it is necessary] to toil through together [with them], both raising and educating [them]; but you seem to me to be choosing the laziest [things].
prose: And besides this, you seem to me to be betraying your own sons as well — whom, though it's in your power to raise and educate them, you will go off and abandon, and as far as you're concerned, they will fare however they happen to fare. And they will meet, in all likelihood, with the sort of things that usually happen to orphans in cases of orphanhood. For one ought either not to have children at all, or to see it through with them, toiling to raise and educate them — but you seem to me to be choosing the laziest way.

literal: But [one] must choose the very things which a man good and brave would choose, these things [one must choose], [one] at least indeed claiming to care for virtue through the whole of life; as I at least, both on behalf of you and on behalf of us your friends, am ashamed lest the whole affair, the one concerning you, be thought to have been done with some cowardice of ours, and the entrance of the suit into the court, how it entered when it was possible not to enter, and the contest itself of the suit, how it came about, and this, the last thing indeed, this here, as it were a laughingstock of the affair, through some wretchedness and through our cowardice [it seeming] us to have escaped — we who did not save you, nor did you yourself [save] yourself, though it was possible and feasible, if there was even some small use from us.
prose: But one must choose the very things that a good and brave man would choose — at least if one claims to care about virtue throughout one's whole life; for I, both for your sake and for ours, your friends, am ashamed that this whole affair of yours may be thought to have been handled with some cowardice on our part — the entry of the case into court, how it was brought in when it could have been avoided, the very conduct of the trial, how that went, and then this last absurd thing of all, as it were a mockery of the business, seeming to have escaped us through some wretched cowardice of ours — since we did not save you, nor did you save yourself, though it was possible and feasible, if there had been even some small use in us.

literal: Crito: . These things then, O Socrates, see lest at the same time with the bad also [it] shameful may be for you and for us. But do deliberate — [it is] rather, and [it is] not still time to be deliberating, but [it is time] to have deliberated — and [there is] one plan. For of-the coming night all this it-is-necessary to-have-been-done, but if still we-shall-wait [it-is], impossible and no-longer possible. But in every way, O Socrates, obey me and in no way do otherwise.
prose: Crito: Well then, Socrates, consider whether this plan might at the same time be both bad and shameful for you and for us. Socrates: No, deliberate — or rather, there's no time left to deliberate, but to have deliberated already; and there's only one plan. For during the coming night all this must be done, but if we wait any longer, it will be impossible and no longer feasible. Crito: But Socrates, do as I say in every way, and please don't act otherwise.

literal: Socrates: O dear Crito, the eagerness of-you [would-be] of-much worth, if with some rightness it-should-be; but if not, by-as-much-as [it-is] greater, by-so-much [it-is] harder. To-consider, then, it-is-necessary [for] us whether both this [thing] is-to-be-done or [0] not; as I not now first but also always [am] such a one as to-be-persuaded by-none other of-my [parts] than by-the argument which, to-me reasoning, appears best.
prose: Socrates: O dear Crito, your eagerness would be worth a great deal if it should be attended by some rightness; but if not, the greater it is, the harder it is to deal with. So we must consider whether this is to be done or not, since I am not only now but always the sort of man who obeys nothing else of what is mine except the argument which, upon reasoning, appears to me best.

literal: The arguments, indeed, which in the former [time] I was saying, I am not able now to throw out, since to me this fortune has come about, but rather similar in some way they appear to me, and the same ones I honor and I esteem whom also [I esteemed] before. Of which [arguments], if we should not have better [arguments] to say in the present [circumstance], know well that I will certainly not agree with you, nor even if the power of the many should frighten us, as [it would frighten] children, with more [terrors] than those now present, sending upon [us] bonds and deaths and confiscations of property.
prose: The arguments, then, which I used to make before, I can't throw out now just because this misfortune has happened to me; rather, they look pretty much the same to me, and I honor and esteem the same ones I did before. Of these, if we have nothing better to say at the moment, be assured that I will certainly not give in to you, not even if the power of the majority should try to frighten us like children with more terrors than it brings now, sending bonds and deaths and confiscations of property upon us.

literal: How then might we most-moderately examine these-things? If first indeed this the argument we-might-take-up-again, which you say about the opinions — whether well it-was-said each-time or not, that to-the some opinions on-the-one-hand it-is-necessary to-pay the mind, to-the but [opinions] not [to-pay-the-mind]? Or, before indeed I must die, well was-it-said, now but has-it-become clear that otherwise for-the-sake of-argument it-was-said, and was-it mere-play and nonsense, as truly?
prose: How then might we most fairly examine these matters, if first we took up again this argument which you make about opinions — whether it was always rightly said or not, that one must attend to some opinions but not to others? Or was it rightly said before I had to die, but now has it become clear that it was spoken only for the sake of argument, and was really just idle play and nonsense?

literal: It-was-said δέ somehow, as I ᾦμαι, each-time thus by-those supposing something to-say, just-as just-now I was-saying, ὅτι of-the opinions which the men opine, it-would-be-necessary the μέν [ones] concerning much to-make [to-value], the δέ [ones] not [to-make].
prose: It was always said, I think, in this sort of way, by those who suppose they're saying something significant — just as I myself was saying a moment ago — that of the opinions which people hold, some ought to be valued highly, but others not.

literal: Socrates: This, by the gods, O Crito, does it not seem to you to be well said?
prose: Socrates: This, Crito, by the gods, don't you think this is well said?

literal: Socrates: — For you, as many things indeed as [are] the human ones, are outside of the being-about to die tomorrow, and not would the present misfortune be deceiving you; Consider, then — does it not seem to you sufficiently to be said that it is necessary not all the opinions, [namely] of men, indeed to honor, but these indeed [ones], but these not, and not of all indeed, but of these indeed [ones], but of these not?
prose: Socrates: — For you, at least as far as human affairs go, are outside the prospect of dying tomorrow, and the present misfortune would not be deceiving you. Consider, then — doesn't it seem to you to be well said that one must honor not all the opinions of men, but some and not others, and not those of all men, but those of some and not others?

literal: What are you saying? Isn't this said well?
prose: What are you saying? Isn't this well said?

literal: Crito. Well [said].
prose: Crito: Well said.

literal: Socrates: So then, the on the one hand good [opinions] honor, but the on the other hand bad [opinions] not [honor]?
prose: Socrates: So then, we should honor the good opinions, but not the bad?

literal: Crito: Yes.
prose: Crito: Yes.

literal: Socrates: Good [are] on the one hand not those of the wise, [but] bad [are] on the other hand those of the foolish?
prose: Socrates: Are the opinions of the wise good, but those of the foolish bad?

literal: Crito: Socrates: How δ' not [so]?
prose: Crito: Socrates: Why not?

literal: Socrates:
prose: Socrates:

literal: Crito: Of one alone.
prose: Crito: [We need to take heed] of one person only.

literal: Socrates: So-then it-is-necessary [to] fear the blames and [to] welcome the praises, not those of-the many, but that of-that one [man] alone.
prose: Socrates: So, then, we must fear blame and welcome praise—not that of the many, but that of that one man alone.

literal: Crito: [They are] clear, indeed.
prose: Crito: That's clear, of course.

literal: Socrates: In this way, then, by him it-must-be-acted, and it-must-be-trained, and it-must-be-eaten, and it-must-be-drunk, in-whatever-way it-seems-good to-the one, to-the overseer and one-who-understands, rather than in-whatever-way to-all the others [it seems good].
prose: Socrates: In this way, then, he must act, and he must train, and he must eat and drink, in whatever way seems good to the one man, the overseer who understands, rather than in whatever way seems good to all the rest together.

literal: Crito: These things are [so].
prose: Crito: That is so.

literal: Socrates: Well, then. But [he], having disobeyed the one man and having dishonored his opinion and his praises, but having honored [the opinions] of the many and who understand nothing, then will he indeed suffer nothing bad?
prose: Socrates: Well, then. But by disobeying the one man and dishonoring his opinion and his praises, while honoring the opinions of the many who understand nothing, will he suffer no harm at all?

literal: Crito: Socrates: For how [is it] not [so]?
prose: Crito: Socrates: Of course it is.

literal: Socrates: And-δ' what is the evil this, and whither does-it-tend, and into what of-the [things] of-the-one-disobeying?
prose: Socrates: And what is this evil, and what does it aim at, and into which of the disobedient person's troubles does it fall?

literal: Crito: [It is] clear that [it tends] into the body. Socrates: For this [it] destroys.
prose: Crito: Clearly it harms the body. Socrates: For this is what destroys it.

literal: Socrates: Is it not so also with the other [things] too, Crito, thus, in order that we may not go through all [of them]—and indeed also concerning the just and unjust and shameful and noble and good and bad [things], concerning which [things] our present deliberation is for us—must we follow and fear it, the opinion of the many, or [must we follow and fear] that of the one [person], if someone is [a person] understanding, whom we must both respect and fear more than all the others [combined]?
prose: Socrates: Isn't it the same, Crito, with the other matters too—so that we don't have to go through them all—and especially with just and unjust, shameful and noble, good and bad things, the very things our present deliberation concerns: must we follow the opinion of the many and fear it, or that of the one person, if there is someone who understands, whom we must respect and fear more than all the others combined?

literal: [That] by which, if we do not follow [it], we will corrupt and we will maim that thing, which indeed through the just became better, but through the unjust was being destroyed. Or is this nothing?
prose: If we do not follow that principle, we will corrupt and ruin that thing which used to become better through justice and was being destroyed through injustice. Or is this nothing?

literal: Crito: I-think, I at least, O Socrates.
prose: Crito: I think so, Socrates.

literal: Socrates: Come δή [then], ἐὰν [if] the on the one hand [μέν] by the healthy made better, but [δέ] by the diseased being destroyed—this we should destroy by obeying not the opinion of those not understanding, ἆρα [then] is it livable for us, it having been destroyed? And που [I suppose] this is a body· or not [is it so]?
prose: Socrates: Come then, if that which is made better by what is healthy, but ruined by what is diseased—if we destroy that by obeying the opinion of those who don't understand, is life worth living for us once that part is ruined? This, I suppose, is the body. Or isn't it so?

literal: Crito. Yes.
prose: Crito: Yes.

literal: Socrates: [-]Then[-]worth-living for-us it-is with wretched and having-been-corrupted body?
prose: Socrates: Is life, then, worth living for us with a wretched and corrupted body?

literal: Crito: Not at all [is it so].
prose: Crito: Not at all.

literal: Socrates: But after-all [is it] worth-living for-us with that [part], [it] having-been-ruined, to-which the unjust-thing on-one-hand does-harm, and the just-thing benefits? Or do-we-consider [it] to-be more-worthless than-the body, that thing, whatever-indeed it-is of-our-[things], concerning which both injustice and justice is?
prose: Socrates: But is life worth living for us with that part ruined, by which injustice does harm and justice benefits? Or do we consider that thing which belongs to us—whatever it actually is, concerned with which injustice and justice exist—to be more worthless than the body?

literal: Crito: [It is] not at all.
prose: Crito: Not at all.

literal: Socrates: But more valuable [is it]?
prose: Socrates: But is it more valuable?

literal: Crito: Much, indeed, [it is so].
prose: Crito: Much more so, indeed.

literal: Socrates: Not therefore, O best one, [must it be cared for] by us so very much what the many will say of us, but [it must be cared for] what the one understanding about just things and unjust [will say], the one, and the truth itself. So that, first indeed, in this [opinion] you are not rightly proposing, proposing that it is necessary for us to care about the opinion of the many, concerning the things just and honorable and good, and of the opposite [things].
prose: Socrates: So then, my excellent friend, we must not care so very much what the majority will say of us, but rather what the one who understands justice and injustice will say—that one person—and the truth itself. So then, first of all, in this respect you are not proposing rightly, when you propose that we must care about the opinion of the many concerning things just and honorable and good, and their opposites.

literal: But indeed, someone might say-indeed-ever, the many are such-as [able] to kill us.
prose: But, someone might well say, the majority are able to kill us.

literal: Crito: [These] things also [are] clear indeed. "For he might say, O Socrates," True things you say.
prose: Crito: These things too are clear, then. "For he might say, Socrates," "You're right."

literal: Socrates: But, O wondrous one, this argument too which we have gone through to me indeed still seems to be similar also as before. And this [point] in turn consider, whether it still remains for us or not — [namely] that not the living is to be made of most [importance], but the living well.
prose: Socrates: But, my dear fellow, this argument we've gone through still seems to me to be the same as it was before. And consider this point too, whether it still holds for us or not: that living is not to be valued most of all, but living well.

literal: Crito. But it remains.
prose: Crito: But it stands.

literal: Socrates: But the [thing], that the same [thing] is well and finely and justly, does it remain, or does it not remain?
prose: Socrates: But the principle that the same thing is good and fine and just—does that remain valid, or not?

literal: Crito: It stands.
prose: Crito: It stands.

literal: Socrates: So-then, out-of the-things agreed [upon], this must-be-considered, whether [it is] just for-me to-try to-go-out from-here, the-Athenians not releasing [me], or [it is] not just. And if on-the-one-hand it-appears just, let-us-try [it]; but if [it appears] not [just], let-us-let [it] go. But the considerations which you mention, concerning both expenditure of-money and reputation and rearing of-children, these, not as truly these [things], O Crito, might-be the-considerations of-those easily killing and bringing-back-to-life, if they-were able, with no sense—of these, [that is], of-the many.
prose: Socrates: So then, on the basis of what has been agreed, this must be considered: whether it is just for me to try to get out of here when the Athenians do not release me, or not just. And if it appears just, let's make the attempt; but if not, let's drop it. As for these considerations you mention, about spending money and reputation and raising children, Crito, I fear these are in truth just the concerns of the sort of people who would casually put men to death, and would just as casually bring them back to life again if they could, with no sense at all—the concerns, I mean, of the majority.

literal: But to-us, since the argument thus turns-out, nothing else must-be-considered than just-what we-were-saying just-now: whether just-things we-will-do, both money paying to-these the-ones who-will-lead-out me from-here, and [giving] thanks, and ourselves both leading-out and being-led-out, or in-truth we-will-do-wrong, all these-things doing; and if indeed we-should-appear doing these unjust things themselves, [it-is] not necessary for-you to-reckon-in whether it-is-necessary to-die remaining and keeping-quiet, nor to-suffer anything else whatsoever, before the doing-wrong.
prose: But since the argument turns out this way for us, nothing else must be considered except just what we were saying a moment ago: whether we would be acting justly in paying money and thanks to these men who will get me out of here, and in ourselves getting out and being gotten out, or whether in truth we would be doing wrong in doing all these things; and if we clearly appear to be doing unjust things by this, then you must not take into account whether it is necessary to die from staying here and keeping quiet, or to suffer anything else whatsoever, in preference to doing wrong.

literal: Crito: Well, you seem to me to speak well, O Socrates, but consider what we should do.
prose: Crito: I think you're right about that, Socrates, but do consider what we should do.

literal: Socrates: Let-us-examine, O good-one, in-common, and if in-some-way you-have to-speak-against, I speaking, speak-against, and to-you I-will-be-persuaded; but if not, stop already, O blessed-one, often to-me saying the same word, that it-is-necessary from-here, [the] Athenians being-unwilling, me to-go-away; since I about much make-it, having-persuaded you these-things to-do, but not [you] being-unwilling. Look, then, indeed, at-the of-the inquiry the beginning, if it-be-said to-you adequately, and try to-answer the thing-being-asked in-whatever-way you-may-think most.
prose: Socrates: Let's examine it together, my good man, and if you have any way to argue against me while I'm speaking, speak up, and I'll be persuaded by you; but if not, stop already, you blessed fellow, telling me the same thing over and over, that I must leave here against the Athenians' will; since I set great store on doing this after having persuaded you, and not against your will. Now look, then, at the beginning of our inquiry, if it's stated to you adequately, and try to answer what's asked in whatever way you think best.

literal: Crito: Socrates: But I will try.
prose: Crito: Socrates: Well, I'll try.

literal: Socrates: In no way do we say [it] must-be-done-wrong willingly, or for-someone, on-the-one-hand, must-be-done-wrong in-some way, but, on-the-other-hand, not? Or [is it] in-no-way, at-least, the doing-wrong neither good nor noble, as often by us also in the former time it-was-agreed? Or all those former agreements of-ours are poured-out in these few days, and long-ago, O Crito, so-then such-great men to one-another with-eagerness conversing we-escaped-notice-of ourselves, from children nothing differing?
prose: Socrates: Do we say that one must in no way willingly do wrong, or that it must be done wrong in one way but not in another? Or is doing wrong in no way good nor noble, as we have often agreed before? Or are all those earlier agreements of ours now poured out in these few days, and have we for so long, Crito, at our age, talking so earnestly with one another, failed to notice that we are no different from children?

literal: Or, more than everything, it is so in this way, just as it was then said to us: both if the many say [so], and if not, and both if it is necessary [for] us to suffer still harsher things than these, and if milder [ones], nevertheless the [act of] doing wrong, at least, happens to be, for the one doing wrong, both bad and shameful in every way;
prose: Or rather, it is absolutely more the case this way, just as it was said to us then: whether the majority say so or not, and whether we must suffer still harsher things than these or milder ones, nevertheless doing wrong is, in every way, both bad and shameful for the one who does wrong.

literal: Crito. We say [so].
prose: Crito: We say so.

literal: Socrates: In no way then is it necessary to do wrong.
prose: Socrates: So one must never do wrong at all.

literal: Crito: Not indeed.
prose: Crito: No, certainly not.

literal: Socrates: [Is it] not, then, even while being wronged, [that one] must retaliate-with-wrong, as the many suppose, since, at any rate, [one] must in no way do wrong.
prose: Socrates: So one must not retaliate by doing wrong even when wronged, as the majority suppose, since one must in no way do wrong.

literal: Crito. [It] does not appear.
prose: Crito: It doesn't seem so.

literal: Socrates: But what, then, [is it]? To-do-wrong is-it-necessary, O Crito, or not?
prose: Socrates: But what then, indeed? Must one do wrong, Crito, or not?

literal: Crito: Not it is necessary, surely, O Socrates.
prose: Crito: That surely isn't necessary, Socrates.

literal: Socrates: But what [is it]? To-do-wrong-in-return, faring badly, as the many say, [is it] just or not just?
prose: Socrates: But what about this? To do wrong in return when wronged, as the majority say—is that just, or not just?

literal: Crito: [It is] not at all.
prose: Crito: Not at all.

literal: Socrates: For the [thing], somehow, doing badly to people, differs in nothing from the wronging [them].
prose: Socrates: For, you know, treating people badly is in no way different from wronging them.

literal: Crito: True things you are saying.
prose: Crito: You're right.

literal: Socrates: Not indeed therefore both to-do-injustice-in-return is-necessary, and not to-treat badly no-one of-men, nor, whatever-it-might-be you-should-suffer at-the-hands-of them. And see, O Crito, these-things agreeing-to, that not, contrary-to [your] opinion, you-agree; for I-know that to-few certain [people] these-things both seem and will-seem. To-whom therefore thus it-has-seemed-good, and to-whom not [it-has-seemed-good], to-these not there-is a-common plan, but [it-is] a-necessity these [men], seeing of-one-another the plans, one-another to-despise.
prose: Socrates: So one must neither commit injustice in return nor do harm to anyone at all, no matter what one suffers at their hands. And look here, Crito—consider carefully as you agree to these things, so that you don't agree against your real opinion. For I know that this seems so to only a few people, and will continue to seem so. Well then, those to whom this has thus seemed good, and those to whom it has not, don't share a common plan, but it's necessary for them to despise one another, seeing each other's plans.

literal: Consider, then, well and very much, you too, whether you share-in and does it also seem-good-together to you, and let-us-begin from-this-point deliberating, that never rightly having it is neither the to-do-wrong nor the to-do-wrong-in-return, nor, suffering evil, to-defend-oneself doing-in-return evil — or do you stand-apart and do you not share-in the starting-point? For to-me both long-ago thus and now still it-seems, but to-you if in-some other way it-has-seemed, speak and teach.
prose: So consider carefully, you too, whether you share this view and agree with it, and let us begin our deliberation from this point: that it is never right to do wrong, nor to do wrong in return, nor, when one suffers evil, to defend oneself by doing evil in return — or do you depart from this and fail to share in this starting-point? For to me, both long ago and still now, it seems so; but if you have come to think otherwise in some way, speak and teach me.

literal: But if you abide by the former [things], listen to the [thing] after this.
prose: But if you are standing by your earlier views, listen to what comes next.

literal: Crito: But I-abide and it-seems-good also to-me; but speak.
prose: Crito: Well, I abide by it, and I agree too; so go ahead and tell me.

literal: Socrates: I am saying indeed in turn the [thing] after this, but rather I am asking: whether [one] must-do the-things which anyone agrees with someone to-be just, or [one] must-deceive [him]?
prose: Socrates: I'm saying this again, what comes next, or rather I'm asking: must one do whatever one has agreed with someone to be just, or must one deceive him?

literal: Crito. [It is] to-be-done.
prose: Crito: It must be done.

literal: Socrates: And are we abiding by the things which we agreed on, [they] being just, or [are we abiding] not?
prose: Socrates: And do we abide by what we agreed on, since it was just, or not?

literal: Crito: Not I-have, O Socrates, to-answer to that-which you-are-asking; for I-do-not understand.
prose: Crito: I don't know how to answer what you're asking, Socrates — I just don't understand it.

literal: Socrates: But in this way consider [it]. If it should happen, when we are about to—for us—from here, whether to run away, whether, however it is necessary to name this, having come the laws and the common [thing] of the city, having stood over [us], should ask—
prose: Socrates: But look at it this way: if, when we are about to run away from here—or whatever one ought to call it—the laws and the commonwealth of the city should come and stand over us and ask—

literal: Or does it seem to you [to be] still possible for that city to be and not to have been overturned, in which, if the judgments, the ones having come to be, have no strength at all, but by private individuals are made both powerless and are destroyed? Socrates: What shall we say, O Crito, in reply to these things and other such things? For many things a man could have [to say], both otherwise and especially [if he were] a speaker, to say on behalf of this law [as it is] being destroyed, which prescribes that the judgments, the ones having been judged, are to be authoritative.
prose: Or do you think it's still possible for that city to exist and not be overturned, in which the judgments that have been rendered have no force, but are made powerless and destroyed by private individuals? Socrates: What shall we say to this, Crito, and to other such points? For a man could say a great deal, especially if he were a skilled speaker, on behalf of this law that is being destroyed, which prescribes that judgments that have been decided are to be authoritative.

literal: Or shall-we-say to them that it-was-wronging — for — us the city and not rightly the case it-judged? This, or what shall-we-say?
prose: Or shall we say to them that the city wronged us and did not judge the case rightly? Shall we say this, or what shall we say?

literal: Crito: This, by Zeus, O Socrates.
prose: Crito: Yes, by Zeus, this is so, Socrates.

literal: Socrates: What then would the laws say? "O Socrates, was indeed also this agreed by us and by you, [that you] would abide in the judgments in which the city judges?" If then at them saying [this] we were surprised, perhaps they would say that, "O Socrates, do not be surprised at the things being said, but answer, since also you are accustomed to make use of the asking and answering. Come, for [tell me], finding what fault with us and with the city, are you attempting to destroy us?"
prose: Socrates: What, then, would the laws say? "O Socrates, was this in fact agreed between us and you—that you would abide by whatever judgments the city rendered?" If we were surprised at their saying this, they would perhaps say, "O Socrates, do not be surprised at what is being said, but answer, since you are indeed accustomed to making use of asking and answering. Come now, what fault do you find with us and the city, that you are trying to destroy us?"

literal: Not first indeed we begot you, and through us your mother took, and your father begot you? Tell [us], then, to these — to us, namely to the laws, to the ones concerning the marriages — do you find fault with something, as that not well they are [arranged]? Not do-I-find-fault, I-would-say. But [do you find fault] with-the [laws] concerning the of-the-one-who-came-to-be nurture and education, in which also you were educated?
prose: Did we not, first of all, beget you, and was it not through us that your father took your mother and begot you? Tell us, then, do you find fault with these laws of ours, the ones concerning marriage, as though they were not well made? I would not complain, I would say. But [do you find fault with] those concerning the rearing and education of the one born, in which you too were educated?

literal: Or not well did order us the laws, those set over this, commanding to-the father, the [father] of-you, you in music and gymnastic to educate?
prose: Or did the laws set over this matter not give good orders to us, commanding your father to educate you in music and gymnastics?

literal: And if this [thing] is so, do-you-think it-is from equal [footing], the just [thing], both for-you and for-us, and whatever-things we might undertake to-do to-you, these-things do-you-think [it-is] just to-do-in-return to-you?
prose: And if this is so, do you think that justice stands on equal terms for you and for us, so that whatever we undertake to do to you, you think it right to do that back to us in return?

literal: Socrates. Or then toward your father was not [it] on equal terms, or toward a master, as also toward a master, if he happened to be yours, so that you might do in return these very things which you might suffer, neither, being spoken ill of, to answer back, nor, being struck, to strike back, nor many other such other things; but toward the fatherland then and the laws will it be possible for you, so that, if we try to destroy you, considering [it] to be just, you too, in turn, will try to destroy us the laws and the fatherland in return, insofar as you are able, and will you say that in doing these things you are doing just things, [you] the [one] in truth caring for virtue?
prose: Socrates: Or was it, then, fair toward your father—or toward a master, if you happened to have one—so that whatever you suffered you might also do in return, neither answering back when spoken ill of, nor striking back when struck, nor many other such things; but will it then be possible for you, with regard to your country and its laws, that, if we try to destroy you, thinking it just to do so, you in turn will also try to destroy us, the laws and your country, as far as you are able, and will you claim that in doing this you are doing just things—you who in truth care for virtue?

literal: Or thus are you wise that it has escaped [notice of] you that [your] mother and [your] father and of [your] other ancestors all more honorable is [your] fatherland, and more august and more sacred, and in greater esteem both among gods and among men who have sense, and that revere [it] one must, and more yield and flatter [one's] fatherland when it is angry than [one's] father, and either persuade [it] or do what things it commands, and suffer, if it commands [one] to suffer anything, keeping quiet, whether to be beaten, whether to be bound, whether it leads [one] into war to be wounded or to be killed, these things must be done, and the just thus stands, and not one must yield nor one must retreat nor one must leave [one's] post, but both in war and in court and everywhere one must do what things the city and the fatherland command, or persuade it by that by which the just has grown [to be].
prose: Or are you so wise that you have failed to notice that one's homeland is more to be honored than one's mother and father and all one's other ancestors, and more revered and more sacred, and held in higher esteem both among gods and among men of sense, and that one must revere one's homeland and yield to it and flatter it when it is angry even more than a father, and either persuade it or do whatever it commands, and submit to suffering, if it orders one to suffer anything, in silence—whether being beaten or being bound, or, if it leads one into war to be wounded or killed, these things must be done, and this is what justice requires—and that one must not yield, nor retreat, nor abandon one's post, but both in war and in court and everywhere one must do whatever the city and one's homeland command, or else persuade it as to what is just by nature?

literal: But [to] use-force [is] not holy, not even against mother nor against father, and much yet less against your country?
prose: ...it is not holy to use force even against mother or father, and much less still against one's country.

literal: Crito: To me, at least, it seems [so].
prose: Crito: It seems so to me, at least.

literal: Socrates: Consider, then, O Socrates, the laws would perhaps say, if we these-things truly say, that not just-things you-are-attempting to-do, which-things now you-are-attempting [to-do]. For we, γάρ, you, having-begotten, having-reared, having-educated, having-given-a-share of-all-things of-which we-were able of-the-noble-things, to-you and to-the other all citizens, nevertheless we-proclaim-beforehand, to-the one-having-made the power of-the Athenians, to-the one-wishing, whenever he-be-examined and he-see the-things in the city, the matters, and us the laws, to-whom not we-may-please, we, [it]-is-permitted, having-taken the things of-himself, to-go-away, to-where he-may-wish.
prose: Socrates: "Consider then, Socrates," the laws would perhaps say, "whether we are speaking the truth in saying this, that you are trying to do something unjust in what you are now attempting to do. For we, having begotten you, raised you, educated you, and given a share of all the good things we could to you and to all the other citizens alike, nevertheless proclaim in advance, by having made it a right for any Athenian who wishes, once he has come of age and seen how things stand in the city and seen us, the laws, that if we do not please him, it is permitted for him to take his belongings and go away wherever he wishes.

literal: And no one of us, of the laws, is in-the-way, nor forbids [it], if anyone of you wishes to go into a colony, if we do not please [him], both we and the city, or [wishes], having gone elsewhere, to settle-as-a-metic, to go thither whither he wishes, having his own things. But whoever of you remains, seeing in what manner we both adjudicate the lawsuits and administer the other things of the city, already we say this one to have agreed in deed with us to do these things which we might command; and we say the one not being persuaded does wrong in three ways, both because to us being begetters he is not persuaded, and because to nurturers, and because, having agreed with us to suffer [these things], he neither is persuaded nor persuades us, if we are doing something not well—we proposing [it] and not harshly commanding [him] to do what we bid, but allowing [him] one of two things, either to persuade us or to do [it]—of these he does neither.
prose: And none of us the laws stands in his way, nor forbids him, if any one of you wishes to go off to a colony, in case we and the city do not please him, or wishes to go and settle elsewhere, going wherever he pleases, keeping his own property. But whoever of you stays, seeing the manner in which we administer justice and manage the rest of the city's affairs, we say that he has thereby already agreed with us in deed to do whatever we command; and we say that one who does not obey does wrong in three ways: because he disobeys us who are, as it were, his parents, and because he disobeys his nurturers, and because, having agreed to obey us, he neither obeys nor persuades us if we are doing something wrong—though we propose it and do not harshly command him to do what we order, but allow him one of two alternatives, either to persuade us or to do it—he does neither of these.

literal: Socrates: To these indeed we say also you, O Socrates, will be held in [these] charges, if indeed you will do the things which you have in mind, and [you] not least of the Athenians, but among those most [of all].
prose: Socrates: We say, then, that you too, Socrates, will be implicated in these charges, if indeed you do what you have in mind, and you not least of the Athenians, but among those most of all.

literal: For not ever, γὰρ, would ἄν [you] at some time, ποτε, beyond all the other Athenians, distinctively, have lived in it; if not, to you distinctively it was pleasing; and not τε ever, πώποτʼ, did [you] go out upon a festival-viewing from the city, except that not once, εἰς Ἰσθμόν, into the Isthmus; and not τε anywhere else, nowhere else; if not somewhere going to campaign; nor τε did [you] ever make any other trip abroad, as the other men [do]; nor δʼ did desire of you take [you] to know of another city or δὲ of other laws, ἀλλὰ but we to you sufficient were, and our city [was].
prose: For you would never have lived here, unlike all the other Athenians, so exceptionally, unless it had suited you exceptionally; and you never once went out of the city to a festival, except once to the Isthmus, nor anywhere else at any time, unless going somewhere on campaign; nor did you ever make any other trip abroad, as other people do; nor did any desire ever seize you to know another city or other laws, but we and our city were sufficient for you.

literal: So [οὕτω] very-much [σφόδρα] [you] were-choosing [ᾑροῦ] us and were-agreeing [ὡμολόγεις] to-be-a-citizen [πολιτεύσεσθαι] in-accordance-with [καθʼ] us, and [τε] the other-things [τά ἄλλα] also [καί], [you] made [ἐποιήσω] children [παῖδας] in [ἐν] it [αὐτῇ], on-the-grounds-that [ὡς] the city [τῆς πόλεως] was-pleasing [ἀρεσκούσης] to-you [σοι]. Still [ἔτι], then [τοίνυν], in [ἐν] the very [αὐτῇ] trial [τῇ δίκῃ] itself it-was-possible [ἐξῆν] for-you [σοι] to-assess-for-yourself [τιμήσασθαι] [the-penalty-of] exile [φυγῆς], if [εἰ] you-were-willing [ἐβούλου], and [καί] the-very-thing [ὅπερ] which now [νῦν] you-are-attempting [ἐπιχειρεῖς] with-the-city-unwilling [ἀκούσης τῆς πόλεως], then [τότε] to-do [ποιῆσαι] [it] with-[the-city]-willing [ἑκούσης]. You [σὺ] but [δέ] then indeed [μέν] were-making-a-fine-show [ἐκαλλωπίζου], as-if [ὡς] not being-vexed [οὐκ ἀγανακτῶν] if [εἰ] it-should-be-necessary [δέοι] [you] to-have-died [τεθνάναι], but [ἀλλά] you-were-choosing [ᾑροῦ], as [ὡς] you-said [ἔφησθα], before [πρό] the [τῆς] exile [φυγῆς] death [θάνατον].
prose: So strongly did you choose us and agree to be a citizen in accordance with us, and besides everything else, you had children in it, on the grounds that the city pleased you. Furthermore, even in the trial itself it was possible for you to propose the penalty of exile, if you had wished, and to do then with the city's consent what you are now attempting to do against its will. But you, at that time, were putting on a fine show of not being distressed if you had to die, but you chose, as you said, death over exile.

literal: Now but not indeed those the arguments are-you-ashamed-of, and-not indeed of-us of-the laws do-you-feel-respect, trying to-destroy [us], but you-are-doing the-very-things-which a-slave the most-base would-do, trying to-run-away contrary-to the compacts both and the agreements according-to which to-us you-agreed to-be-a-citizen. First μὲν οὖν to-us this very-thing answer, whether true-things we-say, [we] saying that you have-agreed to-be-a-citizen according-to us in-deed but not in-word, or not true-things.
prose: But now you're not ashamed before those arguments, and you show no regard for us, the laws, as you try to destroy us, but you're doing just what the lowest slave would do, trying to run away in violation of the compacts and agreements by which you agreed with us to live as a citizen. First, then, answer us just this: are we telling the truth when we say that you agreed to live as a citizen under us in deed, not merely in word—or is that not true?

literal: Socrates: What shall we say in reply to these things, O Crito? [Something] else anything or shall we agree?
prose: Socrates: What shall we say to this, Crito? Or shall we just agree?

literal: Crito: [It is] a necessity, O Socrates.
prose: Crito: It's necessary, Socrates.

literal: Socrates: Something else, then, would [they] say, than the covenants, the [ones] toward us ourselves, and the agreements [that you] are transgressing—not having agreed under compulsion, nor having been deceived, nor having been forced in a short time to deliberate, but in seventy years, in which it was possible for you to depart, if we were not pleasing [to you], and the agreements did not appear to you to be just?
prose: Socrates: So, they would say, are you transgressing anything else than the covenants and agreements you made with us, not having agreed under compulsion, nor having been deceived, nor having been forced to deliberate in a short time, but over seventy years, during which it was open to you to leave, if we were not pleasing to you and the agreements did not seem to you to be just?

literal: Socrates: You, on the one hand, neither Sparta nor Crete did [you] choose—which indeed each time you say [are] well-governed—nor any other of the Greek cities, nor of the barbarian ones, but you went abroad from it less than the lame and blind and the other cripples [go abroad from it]; thus to you especially beyond the other Athenians were pleasing the city and we the laws, [it is] clear that;
prose: Socrates: You never chose Sparta or Crete, which you're always saying are well-governed, nor any other Greek city or foreign one either, but you left it less than the lame, the blind, and the other cripples do—so clearly the city and we the laws pleased you especially, beyond the other Athenians;

literal: For by-what [thing] would [a/the] city please [you], without laws? Socrates: Now-δὲ-δή not will-you-abide-by to-the things-having-been-agreed? Crito: If indeed you-are-persuaded by-us, O Socrates — [it will be well]. And not ridiculous indeed will-you-be, out-of the city having-gone-out. Socrates: [Consider] for-δή, these-things having-transgressed and doing-wrong in-anything of-these, what good [thing] you-will-work for-yourself or [for] the fitting [people], the [people] of-your-own. For on-the-one-hand γε your friends are-likely themselves too both to-flee and to-be-deprived either of-the city or the property to-lose, fairly-somewhat [it is] clear.
prose: For what city could please you without laws? Socrates: So now, really, won't you abide by what has been agreed? Crito: If you'll just listen to us, Socrates. And you will indeed be ridiculous once you have escaped from the city. Socrates: Consider, then, by transgressing these things and doing wrong in any of these ways, what good you will do yourself or your friends. For it is fairly clear that, on the one hand, your own friends are likely to risk fleeing with you themselves too and being deprived either of the city or of losing their property.

literal: And you yourself, first, on the one hand, if into one of the nearest cities you go, either to Thebes or to Megara—for both are well-governed—as an enemy you will come, O Socrates, to the constitution of these [cities], and as many as care for their own cities will look askance at you, considering [you] a corrupter of the laws, and you will confirm for the jurors the opinion, so that [they] seem to have judged the case rightly; for whoever is a corrupter of laws would seem, I suppose, very much to be a corrupter of young, at least, and foolish men, to be.
prose: And you yourself—first of all, if you go to one of the nearest cities, either to Thebes or to Megara, for both are well governed—you will arrive, Socrates, as an enemy to their constitution, and all who care about their own cities will look at you askance, considering you a corrupter of the laws, and you will confirm for the jurors their opinion, so that they will seem to have judged the case correctly; for whoever is a corrupter of laws would surely seem, I suppose, very much to be a corrupter of young and foolish men too.

literal: Whether then will-you-flee both the well-governed cities and of-the men the most-orderly [ones]? And this doing [for you], indeed will-it-be worthwhile for-you to-live? Or will-you-approach these [men] and will-you-be-shameless, conversing — what sort-of words, O Socrates? Or the-very-ones here, as the virtue and the justice is worth most to-men, and both the lawful-things and the laws? And do-you- not -think [that] shameful will-appear the of-Socrates matter?
prose: Will you then flee the well-governed cities and the most orderly of men? And will life even be worth living for you, if you do this? Or will you go up to these people and shamelessly engage them in conversation — saying what, Socrates? The very things you used to say here, that virtue and justice are worth the most to men, and so are lawful customs and the laws? And don't you think that Socrates' case will look disgraceful?

literal: Socrates: [One] must indeed think [so]. But, on the one hand [μέν], from these the places you will depart, and [δέ] you will come into Thessaly, to the friends, [namely] those of Crito; for there, indeed [γὰρ δὴ], [there is] greatest disorder and licentiousness, and perhaps [ἴσως ἄν] gladly they would hear of you, how ridiculously, from the prison, you were running away, having put on some disguise, either a leather-coat having taken, or other things, such as indeed those running away are accustomed to dress themselves up in, and having changed the shape, the [shape] of yourself.
prose: Socrates: Yes, that's exactly what one must think. But you'll leave from this region, and come to Thessaly, to those friends of Crito's? For there, you know, there's the greatest disorder and lack of discipline, and perhaps they'd gladly hear about you — how ridiculously you ran away from the prison, putting on some disguise, either taking a leather jerkin or whatever else people on the run usually dress up in, and changing your own appearance.

literal: That, [you being] an old man, of little time being left to [your] life, as is likely, you dared so greedily to desire to live, having transgressed the greatest laws—[will there be] no one who will say [this]? Perhaps, [provided] you may not be upsetting someone. But if not, you will hear, O Socrates, many things also unworthy of yourself. Fawning, then, [upon] all men and being a slave [to them], you will live—doing what, or feasting, in Thessaly, as having gone abroad into Thessaly as if to a dinner?
prose: Won't there be someone who will say that, old man as you are, with little time of life likely left to you, you dared so greedily to desire to live, having transgressed the most important laws? Perhaps—unless you avoid upsetting anyone. But if not, Socrates, you will hear many things unworthy of yourself. Fawning on all men and playing the slave, you will live out your life—doing what, or rather feasting, in Thessaly, as if you had gone abroad to Thessaly just for a dinner?

literal: Socrates: But those arguments, the ones concerning justice and the rest of virtue, where for us will they be? But indeed, for the sake of [your] children, do you wish to live, in order that you might raise them up and educate [them]? But what [is it]? Into Thessaly [them], having led [them], will you feed and will you educate, having made [them] strangers, in order that they too may enjoy this [benefit]? Or is this [so] not, but, being reared here, you living, better will they be fed and will be educated, you not being present with them?
prose: Socrates: But where will those arguments about justice and the rest of virtue be for us then? But surely you do wish to live for your children's sake, so that you may raise and educate them? What, then? Will you take them off to Thessaly and feed and educate them there, making them foreigners, so that they can enjoy that too? Or is that not the point—rather, will they be better fed and educated by staying here while you're alive, even if you're not with them, than if they're raised without your being present?

literal: For the — your — friends will care for them. Whether, on the one hand, if you go abroad into Thessaly, they will care [for you], but, on the other hand, if you go abroad into Hades, will they not care [for you]? If indeed there is some use of them, of those claiming to you to be devoted ones, [one] ought at least to think [so]. But, O Socrates, obeying us, your nurturers, make neither children nor the living nor anything else to be of more account than the just, so that having gone into Hades you may have all these things to say in defense to the rulers there;
prose: For your friends will take care of them. Will they, if you go abroad to Thessaly, take care of them, but if you go abroad to Hades, not take care of them? If indeed those who claim to be your friends are of any use at all, you ought to think so at least. No, Socrates, obey us, your nurturers, and value neither children nor life nor anything else more than justice, so that when you arrive in Hades you may have all this to say in your own defense before the rulers there.

literal: For not-both for to-you here does-it-seem these-things doing better to-be, nor more-just, nor more-pious, nor to-any-other of-your [people] either; nor, having-arrived there, will-it-be better [for-you]. But now indeed, having-been-wronged, you-go-away, if you-go-away, not by us the laws but by men; but if you-go-out thus disgracefully, both having-wronged-in-return and having-done-harm-in-return, your-own agreements and covenants, those toward us, having-transgressed, and having-wrought evils against these whom it-was least-necessary [to-harm]—yourself and friends and country and us—we will-be-angry at-you living, and there our brothers, the laws in Hades, not kindly will-receive you, knowing that us-too you-tried to-destroy, your part.
prose: For not even here does it seem to you better, or more just or more pious, to do this, nor better for any other of your people either, nor will it be better for you once you've arrived there. But as it is, you will go away wronged—if indeed you go away—not by us, the laws, but by men; whereas if you go out in that disgraceful way, repaying wrong with wrong and harm with harm, breaking your own agreements and covenants with us, and doing harm to these very people whom you ought least of all to have harmed—yourself, your friends, your country, and us—then we will be angry with you while you live, and there too our brothers, the laws in Hades, will not receive you kindly, knowing that you tried, as far as lay in your power, to destroy us as well.

literal: Socrates: But not you let-be-persuaded, Crito, to do the-things-which he-says rather than we [say]. These things, O dear friend, comrade, Crito, well know that I myself seem to hear, just as those corybant-raving seem of-the pipes to hear, and in me this same echo of these words buzzes and makes [me] not able of-the others to hear. But know, as-much, at-least, as the now to-me seeming things [are], if you speak contrary-to these things, in-vain you-will-speak.
prose: Socrates: No, Crito—don't let Crito persuade you to do what he says rather than what we say. These things, dear friend Crito, know well, I seem to hear, just as those in Corybantic frenzy seem to hear the pipes, and in me this very echo of these words buzzes and makes me unable to hear anything else. But know this: as far as what now seems true to me goes, if you speak against it, you'll be speaking in vain.

literal: Nevertheless-indeed, if you-think [that-]you-will-do anything more, say [it].
prose: Still, if you think you'll accomplish anything more, say it.

literal: Crito: But, O Socrates, not I-have to-say.
prose: Crito: But, Socrates, I don't know what to say.

literal: Socrates: Allow [it], then, O Crito, and let us act in this way, since in this way the god is leading [us] on.
prose: Socrates: Well then, Crito, let it be, and let's act this way, since this is the way the god is leading us.
